meta.description: Not Mark Twain. The image is a 200-year-old borrowing from a Sanskrit couplet about sandalwood scenting the axe; a close variant of the wording was credited in 1981 to a man named George Roemisch. The Twain credit first appears in a 1971 newspaper advertisement.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Forgiveness is the fragrance that the violet sheds on the heel that has crushed it'?
meta.ogDescription: A funeral and sermon staple, and not Twain's. The metaphor starts in Sanskrit with sandalwood and an axe; the violet version was credited to George Roemisch in 1981.

answer.label: Not Twain — an old borrowed image with a named modern claimant
answer.authorDates: Anonymous tradition · ancestor image recorded in English in 1794; violet wording credited to George Roemisch, 1981
answer.sourceLine: There is no Twain source — no book, sketch, notebook, letter or reported remark. The picture is far older than he is: Sir William Jones rendered a Sanskrit couplet into English in 1794 about the sandal tree that ‘sheds perfume on the axe which fells it.’ The flower kept changing hands — a floweret in 1845, a geranium in 1869, a violet by 1916 — and a close variant of the modern wording was credited in a 1981 Dear Abby column to George Roemisch. The exact wording people quote today first surfaces in a 1971 newspaper advertisement, which is where the Twain label was stuck on.

docMeta.dd: A borrowed image, not a single author
Sanskrit couplet on sandalwood, in English 1794

source.excerpt: The Sandal-tree, in the instant of its overthrow, sheds perfume on the axe, which fells it.
trail: The oldest form of the thought is not about forgiveness at all, and not about a violet. Sir William Jones, the orientalist, quoted an ancient Sanskrit couplet in 1794 about the sandal tree perfuming the axe that cuts it down. Every later version is a substitution on that one image the chronology ↗.

The flower then wanders through the 19th century: a crushed floweret in 1845, trampled flowers in 1855, a geranium in Sophia May Eckley’s verse in 1869, flowers underfoot in Ella A. Giles in 1890. The violet itself surfaces in The Judge in 1916 — six years after Twain’s death.

The precise wording people quote today has one named claimant. In 1981, a reader wrote to Dear Abby crediting a former schoolmate, George Roemisch, with ‘Forgiveness is the fragrance of the violet on the heel of the one who crushed it.’ That is a decade after the Twain credit began circulating, which is the tell: attributions to famous men usually arrive before the real author is identified, not after.

It is absent from TwainQuotes.com, the sourced database maintained by Barbara Schmidt, and from Mark Twain at Your Fingertips. The earliest located Twain credit is a 1971 Spokane newspaper advertisement; in 1973 the syndicated columnist Hal Boyle repeated the Twain credit with a twist — ‘It was Mark Twain (quoting an asylum inmate) who observed…’ — adding an unverifiable second-hand layer rather than replacing Twain.
source.excerptNote: The ancestor, translated from Sanskrit in 1794. It is a harder image than the violet one: an axe, not a heel; a tree being destroyed, not a flower being stepped on by accident. The softening into a violet and a shoe is what made it preachable.
source.rightsNote: Rights here are genuinely mixed, so we do not give the saying a single status. The 1794 sandalwood rendering and the 19th-century flower variants are long out of copyright and free to reproduce. The exact modern violet sentence is a different matter: if George Roemisch composed it, it is a 20th-century original and its rights sit with him or his estate, not in the public domain — and nobody has ever established the date of composition. Because the line is not Twain’s, his status is irrelevant to it either way. Quote it with an honest attribution rather than treating it as free stock text. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Mark Twain
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Twain
author.bio: Mark Twain is the default author for any unclaimed English sentence that sounds wise, and this one has the extra qualification of sounding like a wounded man being generous — a register Twain really did write in. The catch is that he is also the most heavily indexed American writer alive or dead: TwainQuotes.com and Mark Twain at Your Fingertips exist precisely so that claims like this can be checked, and this sentence appears in neither. With Twain, absence from the corpus is not a shrug. It is close to a verdict.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This one is a favourite at funerals and in sermons, which is exactly why it needs a name attached. The name it got was the wrong one, and it arrived a full decade before the strongest named claimant surfaced.

items.why: Nothing in his books, sketches, notebooks, letters or reported speech. It is missing from TwainQuotes.com and from Mark Twain at Your Fingertips, the two places a genuine Twain line would be. The earliest located Twain credit is a Spokane newspaper advertisement of 1971 the trail ↗.

items.who: The strongest claimant to the modern wording
items.why: A Dear Abby reader named him in 1981 as a former schoolmate who wrote it. That is a real, specific, checkable claim of a kind the Twain credit never had — but it is a second-hand recollection in a newspaper column, not a manuscript, so we hold it as a credit rather than a proof.

items.who: A 1973 embellishment, not a rival credit
items.why: The syndicated columnist Hal Boyle repeated the Twain credit in 1973 with a twist: ‘It was Mark Twain (quoting an asylum inmate) who observed…’ That adds an unverifiable second-hand layer — an unnamed inmate Twain supposedly quoted — rather than replacing Twain. It is a continuation of the 1971 credit, not an independent one.

You will see ‘the fragrance of the violet on the heel of the one who crushed it,’ ‘that the violet sheds upon the heel,’ and versions substituting rose or lily. There is no canonical text, because there is no canonical document.

misattribution.truthLine: An old borrowed image — sandalwood and an axe in Sanskrit, a violet and a heel by 1916 — with the modern wording credited to George Roemisch in 1981. Twain has no connection to it at all the chronology ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It gives forgiveness a physical shape. Not a decision or a duty, but something a crushed thing does automatically — which is the most flattering possible account of an extremely hard act, and why it turns up so reliably at funerals and in eulogies for difficult people.

It also carries a small sting that most quoters miss. The violet has been stepped on. The line does not pretend the injury did not happen; it just insists the response can be sweetness anyway. That is why it survives being read aloud to grieving rooms.
detailsBody: 1794: a sandal tree sheds perfume on the axe that fells it — Sir William Jones, from Sanskrit.
1845: a crushed floweret, in a devotional piece titled ‘Father! Forgive Them!’
1869: Sophia May Eckley uses a geranium.
1890: Ella A. Giles publishes a poem with flowers trampled underfoot.
1916: the violet arrives, in the American humour magazine The Judge.
1971: a Spokane newspaper advertisement credits it to Mark Twain.
1981: Dear Abby prints a reader’s credit to George Roemisch.
context.pull: The Twain credit arrived in 1971. A named claimant surfaced in 1981 — ten years too late to stop it.
